why: BACKSPACE always undoes whatever sits immediately left of the cursor, so the characters left of the cursor behave like a stack of operation records (inserted char or skipped original). Backspace pops the top: an insert is cancelled, a skip becomes a delete. Finally merge adjacent records of the same type.
hints: What is directly to the left of the cursor after each action, and does it come from an APPEND or from the original document?

Record each APPEND as an insert and each successful RIGHT as a skip, pushing the record's index on a stack of live records. BACKSPACE pops the top record: if it is an insert, cancel it; if it is a skip, turn it into a delete (the original character is removed).
One pass builds the record list in O(actions); a second pass drops cancelled inserts and merges neighbours of the same type (concatenate text, add counts), converting counts to strings.
pitfalls: A deleted original stays in the log as DELETE, while a cancelled insert disappears completely; that difference is why you cannot just pop from the output.
RIGHT past the end of the document and BACKSPACE with nothing on the left do nothing and produce no record.
Merge only after cancellation: cancelling an insert between two skips makes them adjacent, and they must merge.
Counts are output as decimal strings, and there is no trailing SKIP for the untouched suffix.
